title: Run & Gun = Run & Die
text:
Socom is a very cool game. I was (and perhaps still am) a [[ASIN:B0016B28WU CoD4]] online junky. Now I have some fresh new junk to get addicted to.

Why would I need Socom if I already have an online shooter that I'm addicted to? Because Socom is truly different. This is a team tactical shooter and CoD4 is run out into the map and kill as many people as you can shooter.

The key to success (for me anyway) in Socom is "stick together".

You play as either a Commando or a Mercenary. Once in a lobby you can switch teams and during intermissions the game will regularly switch your whole team back and forth from Mercenary to a Commando. You can create about 5 Mercenary profiles and 5 Commando profiles; and you can change the weapon loadouts in game.

There are assault rifles, submachine guns, light machine guns, shotties, sniper rifles, and one extra rifle from a group of 5 that are available depending on whether you're in a clan and what clan you're in (Spain, France, Germany, UK or US).

All of the rifles and the following gear and stuff are available to everyone; I don't think there's any unlocking or leveling up needed. Your rewards for quality play instead are status, medals & stars.

The gear is kind of cool, but I'm pretty sure that the best loadout is the simple one: M67 frag grenades. The missile launchers are effective, but cumbersome. The claymores have to be detonated versus the CoD4 kind that blew up if an enemy walked near it. So for now, I'm sticking to the grenades.

One thing to note is that each weapon needs to be equipped. In other words, there's not a dedicated button on the controller to throw a grenade or switch to a launcher. You need to bring your selected secondary weapons up on a display by pressing O. Once a secondary weapon is selected you can switch back and forth between it and a primary weapon by pressing L1 (no, L1 is not your sight button; sight is up on the D pad...and to get off your sight you must press down on the D pad). (You can custom configure the wireless controller to your own liking if you don't like the default or other presets.)

The attachments for your weapons are plentiful: scopes, regular and laser sites, silencers, bipod and grenade launchers. Each attachment is not available on every weapon. And be careful, a laser sight will give away your position in night games.

Oh yeah, night games...you'll need your nightvision goggles for those. Navigating the maps takes a little getting used to, but as I said earlier, you should be pretty much sticking together with your team...follow them and take a position. That's right...there's some camping to be done here...but be smart: stay in one place too long and you'll be dead faster than you can say WTF!

And speaking of dead, I believe that you only get rewards by playing "ranked" matches. Friendly fire is on and there is no respawning. There are 4 v 4 matches, 8 v 8 and higher; so when you play Socom, in some matches you'll be atop the leaderboard with 2 kills. I personally have enjoyed the two smaller group matches, but that's a matter of preference.

So communicate with your team! Someone on your team is probably familiar with the map. Ask where to go. There's no stupid or noob questions here; the players that I've met got more mad when their team members didn't communicate and use their mics than they did when someone says "what should we do?"

Speaking of the mic, I bought the [[ASIN:B001C4DKG4 Stand Alone]] edition of Socom, because I have the [[ASIN:B0009B0IX4 Plantronics Voyager 510 Bluetooth Headset]] and it works great. But if you want to take advantage of all of the perks (like on screen volume and stuff) that were in the PS3 2.5 firmware update, then you should probably go with this edition that includes the new official PS3 Headset.

This game rocks. Some of the maps according to some of the folks that I've played with are carry-overs from past Socom games. That gives Socom vets a bit of an early advantage. But it won't be long before I'm navigating these maps on point instead of following my team.

Buy Socom if you play online.

Side note on initial game installation: If your PS3 is set to auto-start discs you might need to disable that the first time you plug in the disc. After you put the game in, you'll see two icons on the XMB for Socom; one installs the game, the other starts it. Install the game first. For some reason even after you run the installer, the game installer icon doesn't disappear; just be sure to start that game with start icon going forward. After the installation I got an error message that said my "saved data" was corrupted....so I deleted the Socom saved data from the XMB (NOT the "game" data...the "saved" data) and the error message disappeared.

Another side note: As of this writing, there are major server issues. Load delays. Freezes. Choppy action and more. Slant 6 Games NEEDS to fix these. If you release a game that is online only, you should release it when you are ready to set the bar for online gaming...not be a work in progress.

title: Mass Effect Succeeds Again
text:
In this highly anticipated sequel, Commander Shepard continues fighting to save the galaxy, reunite with old friends, and make new ones. Mass Effect 2 does not disappoint and has been overhauled and streamlined in many ways and it is mostly a good thing.

Note: This review is written mostly from the perspective of comparing Mass Effect 1&2 (ME1 received 4 stars-4.5 stars if I could). Hope this review helps.

Pros:
-Controls are intuitive. They are easy to get used to and is context sensitive, meaning there are less keys to learn. E.g. When space is pressed, it can be used to go into cover, run, or interact with an object depending on the context.
-Combat has been streamlined. Weapons sound great and even feel like it is more powerful. Special abilities have a faster cool down period, letting you use them more frequently. Combined with smooth controls, ME2 lets you freeze, burn, throw, and pull your enemies in any combination with ease.
-It is even more cinematic than ME1 and combined with an amazing soundtrack, making it that much more immersive, dramatic, and exciting.
-There are many more characters to learn about and interact with, each with a unique personality that makes them stand out from others.
-Side quests are individually designed and has been given as much care as the main missions themselves.
-All the things that made the previous Mass Effect great are back. The dialogue wheel and decision making is back, great story telling, voice cast, drama, history, and humor are all back.
-Ability to import your saved games from the first Mass Effect.
-Without too many details, how well you play during the whole game affects the outcome of the last mission. This is simply ingenious.
-Beautiful graphics and a great price ($10-$15).

Cons:
-Minor glitches such as walking over crates, occasionally getting stuck.
-As a personal preference, there is less customization in special abilities, weapons, and armor. This is part of the streamlining process in which it may have been oversimplified and makes ME2 head towards the direction of being a straight forward shooter rather than a well balanced RPG shooter. This may please FPS (or third person shooter) enthusiasts, but less so for RPG enthusiasts (assuming you're one or the other). I, on the other hand have mixed feelings and love FPS at the same time. The lack of customizability also leads to less strategy and less trade offs.
-Some special abilities overlap. They may have different names, but generally serve the same purpose. For example, geth shields, fortifications, and barriers are all different abilities, but in terms of functionality, they all give you shields.

Note: If you play ME2 by itself, you may not care for the lack of customizability. Mass Effect 2 still stands alone as a great shooter with a great story.

Mass Effect 2 continues Bioware's impeccable story telling tradition and sets up very well for Mass Effect 3. Mass Effect 2 is very well polished, and depending on where you stand on this RPG shooter spectrum, it may very well be the perfect game. Whether you are a newcomer to the series or a Mass Effect veteran, this is not to be missed. If you played the first Mass Effect and loved the RPG elements, you won't find it here, but the story and the pace of the game will have you so engrossed that you may even forget to miss the RPG elements. Playing Mass Effect 1 before Mass Effect 2 is highly recommended.

title: A Good Last Expansion Pack for the Series.
text:
Though it's a little uneven, this last expansion pack (EP) for the Sims 3 has undeniable charms for someone interested in futuristic, science-fiction Simming.

This EP adds a variety of SF-themed special objects, clothes, and hairs to the game. From "Back to the Future" hoverboards (think "flying skateboards") to jetpacks like Calvin's dad wore in the fantasy segments of the old comic strip, to nanotech research and robot building centers, to weird portals, to the way even the potted plants look like they came straight out of a "Star Trek" reboot movie, there's a lot here to look at and enjoy. It's not going to add a lot to the regular game without completely wrecking its ambience, though, and Simmers who prefer a more medieval, goth, realistic, urban/gritty, or fantasy feel to their game aren't going to appreciate a lot from this EP. The decor and new wall/floor textures are to say the least utilitarian, and while it's all utterly thematic to a science fiction experience, it's not very useful elsewhere--except for transparent glass panel flooring tiles that I love in club venues and grass-textured "carpets" that can be used indoors in greenhouses (thus eliminating unwanted "unfinished room" moodlets)--YAY! Those are extremely welcome.

A new "life state" is introduced here: PlumBots, which are playable robots that can be built ingame from components and whose personalities are determined by chips installed into them. There's a lot of variety to these bots; they can be very simple and sticklike to very complicated and stolid, and of course can be just about any color you want. With the appropriate chipset, they can do just about anything that a regular Sim can do--but their limitations can make them quite a lot of fun all on their own.

And of course there are new collectibles added by the EP. Nanites, new insects, special digsites and the like pepper the landscape. A new style of refrigerator/sink can synthesize the EP's new recipes quite easily as well. New skills include playing a SF-style harp, flying with the jetpack, and eating bugs.

Once the EP's special world (Oasis Landing) is visited, one can easily see the influence of pop SF like "The Hunger Games" in the clothes and hairs, but as with most of the series, sly references are inserted regarding everything from "Futurama" and "Castle" to "Game of Thrones." There's even an old hermit in robes living in a little cabin by himself at the edge of a bleak desert with a name suggesting a certain fellow from an iconic SF movie from years ago. The city itself looks completely inorganic and planned, with flat terrain, carefully laid out roads, and swathes of solar cells in fields. But stray from the city and you'll find a very different picture; the have-nots live in little mining neighborhoods or out in what looks for all the world like the Dune Sea, where treasures await the ambitious--and where a downed spacecraft bears secrets of its own. Even more entertainingly, anything significant your Sims do in the "real" world can influence how their descendants do--and even how that future world looks. And of course your Sims can visit those descendants and interact with them all.

I will say that I pretty much hate almost every single bit of clothing and hair in this EP. The rabbitholes are GORGEOUS and I love the venues EA has made, and their premade Sims/households are as usual outstanding and cheeky. But the clothing and hairs are just ugly to me. Your mileage may vary. It all looks like it was designed by Lady Gaga after watching "The Hunger Games" on auto-repeat for a few weeks.

All in all, if you like science-fiction Simming, you'll like this EP. If you don't like that stuff, chances are you won't really enjoy this EP as much. I held off on getting it for a long time and picked it up only once it went on serious sale, and I'm generally happy with what it's brought my game for the price I paid. I haven't used much of it in my normal gaming though. This is a very specific EP aimed at a very specific audience and it's not going to appeal to absolutely everybody, but if you're one of those people, then you can purchase it in confidence.

title: Switches Between Two Paired Devices; Richer Sound, Clearer Voices From Sony Bravia TV
text:
This BOSE SOUNDLINK COLOR BLUETOOTH SPEAKER may not be the ideal portable speaker for serious audiophiles--because it has no treble/base buttons, only volume buttons--but I love mine. The sound is rich and full, whether it's paired with my old Sony Bravia TV, iPad2, or Kindle Fire, or connected by AV stereo cable (3.5mm M/M) to my MP3 player's headphone jack. The volume is controlled by the device the speaker is connected to, or by the plus/minus volume buttons on the speaker itself. The speaker also has an Aux button for the direct cable connection, and a Skip button that lets you go forward or backward in your music selections.

This Bose portable speaker can support two Bluetooth-connected devices at once, so you can switch between two devices (e.g., an iPad and a Kindle Fire) without repeating the pairing process every time. A great feature! The speaker automatically connects with the last-connected Bluetooth device, and switches devices when you press the Bluetooth button. The speaker's voice prompts help you with pairing, and tell you which two devices are currently paired. The voice prompts can be disabled, if you wish.

This Bose speaker is definitely an improvement over the speakers built into my old Sony Bravia TV. Voices are much clearer--including the dialogue from British TV shows--and the sound is far richer. Of course, using this speaker instead of a TV sound bar is only a temporary solution, because the speaker needs regular recharging. When fully charged, it delivers sound for many hours (up to 8) and outlasts the charge on the [[ASIN:B004B8GF7Y TaoTronics® Bluetooth Transmitter]] that I added to my non-Bluetooth-enabled TV.

Whether the TaoTronics transmitter was connected to the TV's headphone jack or to the TV's AV ouputs, this speaker paired instantly. However, when the TV transmitter was connected to the AV outputs, the speaker produced some static unless it was positioned close to the TV. When the TV transmitter was connected to the headphone jack, the speaker produced no static at all, no matter where it was positioned (within the Bluetooth range).

This Bose speaker charges quickly with the included AC adapter and USB cable. Pressing the speaker's power button produces a battery indicator that glows red, amber, or green to indicate the current level of charge. The speaker is lightweight enough to carry around in a backpack or tote bag. There is a case available (see [[ASIN:B00NJGRKG4 Bose SoundLink Color carry case]]), but I don't think a case is needed, because the speaker seems to be sturdily constructed.

title: The SNK legacy lives on!
text:
King of Fighters Dream Match 99 (KOFDM99) is my current favorite of all the King of Fighters titles (though Garou:Mark of the Wolves is my favorite SNK fighter overall), and that says a lot.
Basically, KOFDM99 is really the Dreamcast version of the Neo Geo game of KOF98:The Slugfest. This confuses a lot of people. KOFDM:99 and King of Fighters '99 Evolution (which is the real KOF99) are two totally different games.
KOFDM99 has just about EVERY character that ever appeared in an official King of Fighters game. That's a whole 38 distinct characters, if you're keeping score. This is the definitive King of Fighters title, and probably the best for 2-player competitions.
KOF99:Evolution and KOF2000 have their merits, but because of their smaller rosters and modified style, they fall a little short of KOF:DM99. While KOF:99E has better effects on the DC (KOF2000 has yet to be ported), KOF:DM99 still holds it own. The graphics easily take on the like of Capcom's greats like SF:Alpha 3. Obviously it doesn't have the pizzazz of the newer 2D DC fighters, the gameplay and character design has always set SNK apart from Capcom or Arc Systems (makers of Guilty Gear).
SNK has always had the most colorful roster, each character distinct with their own robust (if sometimes disturbing) personality that fuels the game. Coupled with good animation, great music, and top-notch controls (minimal learning curve) anyone who considers themselves a 2D fighting fan NEEDS this title. King of Fighters may not be as popular as Capcom's titles, but in Japan it's still one of the most popular series around and for good reason. KOF:DM99 continues the legacy of excellent SNK fighting games.

title: A great addition to the family.
text:
For years I have been using the MX 518. It's a fantastic mouse, but there have been many upgrades and additions to mouse technology since then. I've been drooling over other mice, namely from Razer, Zowie, and Logitech; Logitech has the best general mice, though they may not have as many fancy features as others. Still, if you want a sturdy mouse that will last you years, Logitech is the way to go.

The G502 combines the best of all mouse worlds for me. It's got a braided cord, combines my favorite colors in their scheme, has a two-way scroll wheel WITH BUTTON, different DPI buttons, forward and backward buttons, and an additional side button. It also has two buttons behind the scroll wheel, but one is dedicated to the wheel mode setting. There's also a longer groove on the side for the thumb to rest, and it's more comfortable than the one on my MX 518. The wheel tilts to allow side scrolling, but it never works for me the way I want it no matter how I change the settings.

I had an Anywhere MX mouse and I HATED the wheel. I much preferred the MX 518 scrolling, and still kind of do. The Proteus uses the same wheel type as the Anywhere, but the clicking isn't as forceful; it's still harder than the MX 518, but I've actually gotten quite used to it now.

The left mouse button is shorter and higher than the right one, and that's perfect for me as I have a semi-claw grip. The "G" icon does indeed have a bright light, but it's never bothered me. Either way, you can change the setting to how long it stays on while idle or to shut off permanently.
I'll get to the weights in a bit.

But the best feature? For me at least it's the reprogrammable buttons.
I've reprogramed the wheel button and the one behind, as well as the additional button in front of the forward button. The forward and backward buttons I've kept the same, and I'm glad to report that they're much better stationed than the one on my MX 518. The MX forward button caused me to slide my hand to reach it, whereas I can easily reach both on the Proteus without removing my hand from the mouse.
The lip is very comfortable for my thumb, and provides more of a rest than my previous "gaming" mouse.

Now for the weights.
They come with the mouse in this neat little case. The bottom of the mouse opens extremely easily, but it's sturdy enough so that it won't come undone on its own. There's no tactile or audible click or anything, but you'll tell when the bottom is securely back on. I've used only one weight so far and I'm pretty satisfied with that. I tested it over a week with different weights before deciding on my own preference.

Most of the mouse is made of plastic as you'd expect, while the sides have this nice rubber texture for better grip. It's not the sort of rubber that will show dead skin easily, so no worries there. This is my first mouse with a braided cable, and I'm quite pleased with its lightweight maneuverability thus far.

Overall I'm very pleased. It's everything I wanted in a mouse, and a worthy upgrade to my MX 518. I keep the latter at work now.

I'm not a gaming expert; I just wanted a comfortable mouse that'll be perfect for all my normal tasks, and will prove competent for my Steam gaming.
There are some pretty good wireless mouses out there, but I always tend to stick with corded when possible to decrease computer error. Same applies for my video games The Proteus couldn't have come at a better time, as I've only recently started to consider upgrading my mouse. I'm glad I waited, despite how new this is. It answers all my needs.

title: Was wanting more...
text:
I can't help but feel disappointed with this game. I was hoping for something unique, but what I found was another gear based questing/dungeon/PVP game. SWTOR's biggest new advancement is full voice acting. That is a cool new feature, for a while. But, I found it bored pretty quickly. I still think it's a great new addition to the MMO genre, but it did start to get old. I truely felt underwhelmed. This is the only MMO I've played so far that didn't meet my expectations.

I suppose what I was looking for was the gear based questing/dungeon/PVP WoW model with some sandbox elements. My first MMO was Star Wars Galaxies. You had a huge amount of freedom in that game. SWTOR is very linear and confining. There isn't much to do in the game other than quests/dungeons/PVP. I stumbled into an auditorium, and I was thinking, "Cool, players can make shows and have weddings here.". But, you can't even sit in the chairs. Why even make an auditorium and not allow players to sit down to enjoy some player created content?

There is currently no player housing. I knew people in SWG that redecorated their houses every few weeks. It was a big deal to some people. You could orient items however you liked, and people were so creative. I remember walking into a house and they had taken boulders and made it look like a cave. I was blown away. We use to have block parties, weddings and fashion shows, ext. We use to have guild wars and could set up turrets to help defend the town. You could craft in your house, then put them up for auction while still in your house with vendors that you set up.

I haven't seen any cosmetic clothing yet. Maybe I just haven't leveled high enough, but I haven't seen it yet. For role players, this is kind of a big deal. Sometimes it was an achievement like getting a full set of stormtrooper armor and a carbine so you could walk around feeling like a stormtrooper. Even people like me who don't role play enjoy having something different to wear to distinguish you from the crowd. In WoW, once I got my raid set, that was about it.

The character and race selection is horrible. I didn't find only having four body types to be that big of a deal. But, I didn't like the hairstyles at all. And, the little extras like tattoos or horns were all so similar you really couldn't distinguish yourself. And, all the races were human. No Wookies, Rodians, ext. It just feels so confining.

So what's the big deal about role playing or sandbox elements? I worry that the community will become what WoW's community has become. A bunch of kids or elitist punks. I've been playing LOTRO the past few months, and I don't think I've heard the word "noob" or "pwned" once. It's kind of like the difference between going to a fine dinning restaurant and your local McDonalds. You don't find a lot of screaming kids in a fine dinning restaurant. If you want a more mature playerbase, then you have to give them the tools to do other things than obsess on gear and who's 1337.

The graphics weren't great, but I was expecting that. They aren't bad either. I can't say they were disappointing to me because they were about where I expected them to be. Not everyone has a maxed out system after all. I once bought a laptop and couldn't get it to play WoW. I had to return it and get an upgraded model. So, I know they were trying to get the maximum amount of people whose systems could handle it. I can't fault them on that.

Ambient sounds are missing from the game. And I've heard very little of the original soundtrack. Playing Star Wars Galaxies and hearing the original soundtrack really made me feel like I was in the Star Wars universe, and I was missing that in this game. I guess I kinda miss the whole timeline from the movies as well. I miss seeing stormtroopers and AT-AT's and the like. I just didn't feel immersed in the Star Wars universe that I know and love. It's someone elses Star Wars universe, not the one I grew up with.

Not sure still if I like the group questing in dungeons (flashpoints). Did one with a person that was lagging pretty bad, and we constantly had to wait for him because you all have to talk to the NPC to get quest dialog at the same time. It made for a terribly long and boring dungeon. We could have talked to the NPC and cleared trash while he caught up if we weren't all required to talk at the same time.

The space combat is just a mini game. I think I saw that they may add a more robust space aspect to this game in the future. Which is fine, Star Wars Galaxies didn't launch with a space feature at all. But, if it is going to remain as just something to kill time, that would be very disappointing. Space is a huge part of Star Wars. If I wanted to play a mini game I would sit down and play a hand of Sabaac with another player...if I could sit down. I hope this gets addressed soon in a meaningful way.

Don't get me wrong, I enjoy questing and dungeons and PVP. I just want....more. I am the type of person that tries to complete every quest, even if they are grey. Most of the things I mentioned like sitting down in chairs, player cities and bases and cosmetic clothing are simply tools and really wouldn't effect the gameplay at all. And, they still may add them in later. But, I don't want to be dragged along for years hoping they'll add them, and they never do. I think I'm going to wait a few months to see what direction they are going in before I put down money on a monthly subscription.

title: Pleasantly Surprised by this Router
text:
After my Netgear router decided to degrade to the point of uselessness I set out to replace it and researched several different routers. After looking at a number of reviews online and looking for any information I could find on mid-range wireless N routers I decided to try the MediaLink router. The number of good reviews on this router led to this decision, and so far all of these positive reviews have been justified from my perspective.

Without reading the directions and without running the setup software I had this router online and working with my network in only a few minutes. I did things a little out of order though - I allowed each of my devices to connect to the router first, then I connected the router to the cable modem after which everything worked without any issues.

Tapping into the router's configuration settings is simple, especially since instructions to do so are included. Once in the user is presented with a very simple and self-explanatory menu system that is easy to navigate. In no time at all I had my DHCP reservations set for each device (useful when connecting printers to the wireless network), I had my security key set and had my SSID set for the network.

So far, the router has been stable and fast. In addition to having good network speeds, booting up the router takes very little time - 10-15 seconds, maybe? This is far and away faster than my previous routers.

I have found only a couple of minor drawbacks with this router, neither of which are really problematic but are just things I have noticed. First, I have observed that the signal strength is a little weaker than my previous routers. The router is on the top floor of the house and the main computers I use are in the basement, with one floor in between. While the systems can see the router and connect to it with no issue, the reported signal is not as strong as other routers I have used in the past. Second, and this is a nitpick, I have a dual-boot box that has Windows 7 and Linux on it. When connecting with Windows, the router recognizes the box by its name, but when I connect with Linux it has no name at all - even when I reboot from Windows into Linux immediately.

The MediaLink wireless N router is a decent router that seems to live up to the numerous good reviews it is getting. It seems to be fast and stable and so far I have had no troubles with it at all. The price is very reasonable. If you need a decent and affordable wireless router and you're willing to try a less-familiar name, consider giving this router a try.

text:
Apparently, people are too caught up in the hype of the game to notice the huge flaws.

5. Each level is basically a copy of the level before
4. No challenge at all
3. A microscopic amount of new, good content
2. You can close your eyes and still beat the bosses
1. Moons are a lousy excuse for content

Okay, let me explain myself with a bit of background information on the game. Like ALWAYS, you have to save Princess Peach from the clutches of Bowser. You chase him and his flying boat throughout the world in your hat ship, The Odyssey, by collecting moons to power it. That's basically the entire point of the game, collect moons, beat an easy boss, move on to the next level, and repeat. Over and Over and Over again, a never-ending treasure hunt. What makes it even worse is the fact that the levels hardly change throughout the game. Sure, the actual geography changes, but nothing else. Talk to toad - Get a moon, Ground pound the ground - Get a moon, Hit a rabbit with your hat, twice - Get 3 moons. Since there is hardly any content in the game, they have hundreds of moons that all take little to no effort to get at all, and the way you get them is the same way every in every level. You expect to find moons in all of the exact same ways throughout all the levels. There is nothing challenging or exciting and nothing has driven me to ever actually want to explore this game. I played for six hours total and got almost 700 moons. I like to 100% games and I would have rather played Dark Souls II 999 times (one for each moon) than continue playing this dreadfully boring game. I don't know how adults are getting their jollies from this game because I'm 15 and the flashy colors and cartoon graphics aren't brainwashing me.

Good things

The light and all of its accessories, except the tripod, fit within a great padded, easy to carry, case. The case has padding built into both outer sides and a middle divider. It is complete with heavy duty zippers, handles and an adjustable shoulder strap.

If you are looking for a light that will take your photography to another level, look no further. This is a set you are guaranteed to love.

title: This Is A Lifesaver No Joke!
text:
I read all the reviews and worried about using a collar on my Min Pin service dog. I saw the photos of a dog who got a rash and read reviews that it had no effect on other small dogs. I have never used a collar of any kind on my dog and worried that it might be uncomfortable. However, I became desperate due to his increasing anxiety with construction around us. He began whining and hiding and was inconsistent with his tasks that he usually loves to perform for me. A veterinary behaviorist evaluated him and recommended an Adaptil Collar but I tried the spray instead. When the spray helped, I ordered an Adaptil Diffuser--which also helps indoors. But suddenly my dog began barking at strangers and unfamiliar dogs. He lost interest in his favorite treats and pastimes. I got help from his trainer and tried behavioral training for the triggers. Things were improving a bit then yesterday, just before the collar arrived, something frightened him (I don't know what) and he managed to escape from his harness and run naked through a crowded and heavily trafficked shopping plaza where I had just undergone a medical procedure. I prayed if I ever got my dog back, through a miracle, I would use the Adaptil collar when it arrived. It is truly a miracle that I have my dog back. He was so spooked that he didn't come when I called. He ran up to a building across heavy traffic and a woman brought him into her office, when she saw him running on the railed deck. Luckily, her office was below a dog groomer's place and the groomer was helping me look for my dog. I was still sedated from the medical procedure, and in a wheelchair, but the able-bodied groomer called my dog's name and whistled for him to come. The woman who had my dog heard the man call and returned my dog to me just in time for dial-a-ride to take us home.

I have never used a collar on any animal and worried this would be difficult. It is super easy. There are also videos on YouTube that demonstrate.

I got the small size made for dogs and puppies, recommended for his breed, and it fits perfectly.

He loved the scent the minute I opened the box (I can't smell anything) and even bent his head so I could slip it on. You slip it over their head and adjust it afterwards.

The new upstairs neighbor was making a lot of noise moving in but my dog didn't whine or hide. He cuddled up beside me, closed his eyes, and went to sleep amid all the commotion.

I know there are other calming collars out there but I haven't tried them. I'm sticking to what works. Sentry makes a calming collar that a friend recommended--I didn't like the color for my boy dog and don't want to smell lavender. Plus, his veterinary behaviorist and his vet only recommend Adaptil.

The instructions say keep it on at all times except when grooming. It is very lightweight, soft and pliable and will break free if caught (a concern I had).

It may not work for every dog but if you are desperate like I was, try it. Read the directions. Follow the directions. Don't make the collar too loose or too tight (should be able to insert 2 fingers). If too loose it won't work because depends upon the dog's body heat. And if too loose or too tight it might cause irritation from twisting, turning and rubbing.

So far it works. The next step would have been prescription Paxil--I don't want my fur baby medicated.

It works but remember it's not all we are doing. My dog has regular training with a service dog trainer and we also use the Adaptil spray and Adaptil diffuser. Perhaps it's working because it's part of a whole anti-anxiety program designed by his veterinary behaviorist, who knows and understands him.

title: Appropriately sized food bowl for small pets but I dislike the removable rubber ring
text:
NOTE: Amazon combines reviews for all the DII bowls of this style. This review is for their smallest bowl which is the [[ASIN:B01NCM9PT4 DII Bone Dry Non-Skid Ceramic Pet Bowl For Food & Water, Small - Gray Stripes]]. However, I also own two of their larger bowls [[ASIN:B01N0R11SJ DII Bone Dry Non-Skid Ceramic Pet Bowl For Food & Water, Set of 2, Medium - Nautical Blue Stripes]] which I mention at the end of this review as well.

This small bowl holds a half cup of cat, dog, or other pet kibble comfortably with the food coming a little bit below the rim. The rubber ring on the bottom prevents the dish from moving. The ring is removable and is almost watertight. I wash my dishes by hand and only a few drops of water got between the rubber ring and the bowl bottom. I would have preferred a sealed rubber ring instead of a removable one because I still have to remove the rim to dry underneath which is a hassle.

Overall I like the bowl but I feel the price is high at $8.99 and would have preferred the rubber fully sealed. Other than this, the bowl is heavy, immovable, and holds enough kibble for one small cat or dog. I think it is too small to use for water, however.

PS: I also own their [[ASIN:B01N0R11SJ medium bowls]] and prefer them over the small one above. The reason is that they hold 1-1/2 cup of kibble if filling just below the rim or 2 cups if filling to the top. The medium bowl is also better for water for small pets but I still would not have this as my only water bowl if I were gone from my house more than a few hours. The rubber ring is tighter on the medium bowls. That is both a positive and negative. Positive because it is more watertight and negative because if water does get below the rubber ring, I have to remove it to dry it and then struggle to get it back on. At $21.99, the medium bowls are expensive for two. However, these are good quality bowls that feel hefty and stay put due to the removable rubberized bottom.

I attached two pictures from the front and from the top. Their small bowl is to the left in both pictures and the medium bowls are to the right.

title: Great for my dogs
text:
Great for my dogs. While neither of my dogs is a breed that is in danger of "bloat" significantly, I was concerned about the speed with which they were wolfing down their food. One dog in particular would sometimes throw up a little bit after gobbling an entire meal in one minute.

I've used this now with both dry kibble and with moistened food, and after some work, both dogs are able to get the bowl entirely clean.

To increase their interest in doing the necessary work when I give them dry kibble, I add into the dry kibble a few broken up pieces of a high flavor treat such as a "train me treats" (1.5 cal each). I particularly put these at the outer periphery of the bowl, where it's harder to get the food out.

It now takes my dogs approximately 15 to 20 minutes to eat a meal. There has been no gagging or vomiting since I started using these clever bowls.

I recommend putting the bowl on a mat – – even though there are little rubber pads on the bottom, it will slide around a smooth kitchen floor.

title: Return to PopoloCrois
text:
I've played Harvest Moon games, now generally known as Story of Seasons, but I've not heard of PopoloCrois before, but that's not affecting my game play. If I were to compare this with anything, I'd undoubtedly say this is a bit like Rune Factory, which takes a core RPG and adds a bit of Harvest Moon features. This is heavily story-driven and the farming aspects are sorta taking backseat to everything else. It's also very slow starting, so be prepared to invest some time before you get into full swing. Even at 5 hours play time, I've not fully unlocked everything, and I'm trying to keep myself from looking up spoilers so I don't quite know how long the game is. But being one of the rare types of newer games that included a full-color manual, I know that I've still unlock StreetPass.

The game is probably pretty niche and there's nothing wrong with that. For myself, I find myself feeling a bit blasé about recent big-name releases, so this is a refreshing change of pace. There's not a cast of thousands, characters whose names I can't remember or even care about. It's not epic. It has nice colors and music, a handful of quirky characters (so far), and an overall feeling of classic JRPG game play. I keep saying "so far" or "right now", since I don't know how the game progresses, but 'right now" I have a four-member party who are searching for some number of dungeons to clear so I can progress. Movement is visually similar to classic JRPGs, with an isometric view of with your characters travelling the world and having random encounters. That's where I shudder; I guess games like Pokemon or the older, classic Final Fantasy games have given me an aversion over random encounters. You can adjust the rate, but I still have it set at the highest (which I think was the default).

Combat is decidedly JRPG: an off-world zone with a grid pattern and turn-based combat. You can toggle auto-combat or manual combat, and I've been running mostly on auto with no real problems. If I'm annoyed by the high rate of random encounters, I turn it to manual combat and select "run", but you can lose gold if you run from an encounter.

Well, I won't go on, but if you want something that's pretty stress-free, that won't cause you to rage-quit or tempt you to throw your 3DS against a wall, this is a very nice change of pace.

title: Gorgeous Palette- Works Best With Eye Shadow Base
text:
I am a makeup artist. That means that I use all sorts of makeup from drugstore to high level professional. There are many things about eye shadow that I look for which determine if it is something I can recommend.

HOW THIS COMES
This came with no padding, no protection in a plastic mailer with no bubble cushioning. There is a plastic sheet over the surface of the eye shadow and no mirror in the case. There is no brush.

COLORS
The colors are beautiful. They have nuances that are very difficult to capture on camera. There are matte and shimmer colors- some of which are duochrome- something I look for in shadows.

HOW TO USE THESE
These eye shadows (like almost all other brands of shadow from professional down to drugstore) are best used with a very good eye primer. That will keep them in place and keep them intense too. The only eyeshadow I have ever come across which can be used without a primer and great success is Viseart.

QUALITY
These eye shadows are on a par with the high end cosmetics you find in the more expensive sections of makeup departments. They have a good amount of pigmentation and are velvety smooth too including the mattes.

MATTES
The mattes are not chalky, but are smooth and velvety. They show up well but again, these are best used with a primer.

SHIMMERS
These are some of the most gorgeous shimmer colors I have seen in a while. The collection compliments each other beautifully and look stunning on the eyes and even just in swatches.

ANY ISSUES
I have very sensitive eyes and these shadows did not cause any burning, watery eyes, or irritation of any kind the two days I wore them.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This set of eye shadows is gorgeous. For the price, it is excellent quality and is on a par with shadows much more expensive than these are.

MY RATING
I LOVE these shadows. The colors are gorgeous, quality excellent, and performance above most other shadows in this price range- just be sure to get a good eye shadow primer.

title: A Disappointing Camera From Samsung {Edited}
text:
My first impression upon unboxing this camera was "Wow, that feels cheap." Everything's made from unattractive plastic. The single dial on the top rear of the camera (oddly blank) feels light, spins too easily and clicking it feels mushy. The other buttons on the camera, power, movie and flash all have the same, cheap, mushy feel. The shutter button has poor tactile feel.

The camera is surprisingly heavy; for me uncomfortably, painfully, so.The back is so taken up by the huge 4.8" LCD screen that the thumb rest is too short, more of an afterthought that cause me quite a bit of discomfort during extended use. The DSLR style handgrip is quite large (perhaps too large for small hands) to accommodate the massive 4360 mAh battery.

On paper the idea of an Android OS with a 4.8" LCD screen and a big APS-C sensor sounds great but I was sadly less than impressed.

Because of the Android OS startup time from fully off to ready to shoot is a very long 23 seconds. In standby mode the camera was ready to shoot in approx. 4 seconds. The camera runs warm, very warm, even just sitting idle on a cool 50 degree day. I would worry about overheating in the summer months.

Image quality was unimpressive especially in low light. Early morning, post sunrise, images with sky and clouds were extremely grainy and noisy. Performance in full light was better but not spectacular. Auto focus was run of the mill, often seeking excessively in low light situations. High ISO performance was exceedingly poor. Past ISO 800 images were rather noisier and grainy. In auto mode the camera seemed to make poor choices for ISO and shutter speeds.

Controls. Almost every setting is accessed via the large LCD screen.

There are over twenty pre-configured shooting modes. I used several of them while checking out this camera. These selections are made from a top to bottom scrolling 'carousel' where you scroll through until you find the option you want. I found it annoying to find and stop on the mode I wanted. You're going to miss shots trying to find the mode you want.

Continuous Shooting: burst mode. Surprisingly fast.
Kids Shot: the camera plays one of three sounds to attract a child's attention and then bursts five photos.
Macro: The Galaxy NX has a surprisingly short minimum focal distance with the kit lens and the macro photos I took were among the best results I was able to get from the camera.
Rich Tone: Samsung's HDR mode. Processing time was excessive.
Panorama: This is a sweep mode, smoothly move the camera (a tripod helps) to capture up to 180°'s of view. Disappointingly the camera reduces the image size significantly in Panorama mode.
Multi Exposure: combines two or more images into one.
Drama: combines several images of a moving subject into a single image. The camera was very picky about detecting moving objects. I encountered at least a 50% fail rate trying this mode. Additionally, as with the Panorama mode the image size is greatly reduced.

The camera can also be used in manual mode. Samsung calls it 'Expert Mode'. This gives you access to the standard PASM controls. The settings are controlled by three half-circle on screen dials that I found frustratingly hard to use. Try to change one and my thick fingers would spin the wrong dial. Using Shutter Priority mode I found the processing time of 30 second exposures was a disappointing additional 30 seconds.

There are some things I did like about this camera. It's not all bad. It can produce decent images and I honestly think the majority of the limitations I experienced were due to the cheap kit lens. The 4.8" LCD is gorgeous, in the right light, I recently went back to a camera with a beautiful 3" screen and it felt small. Some of the included shooting modes are fun to play with. Connectivity via WiFi was rock solid (I wasn't able to test the 3G/4G connectivity) even in parking lots of places that offered free WiFi. There were eleven gigs of free space in internal memory. That was plenty of room for a day's shooting and testing. I never did get around to installing an SD card.

In conclusion...
I'm not really sure who this camera is aimed at. They seem to be trying to attract smart phone users with the ability to access the internet almost anywhere and instantly share you photos. But do you really need an expensive, heavy and complex large-sensor camera to post photos to Facebook and Twitter?
On the flip side I just can't see this camera being attractive to professional photographers or high end photography enthusiasts. While the inclusion of the electronic viewfinder is nice I found the all on-screen controls to be distracting and bothersome and the image quality was for the most part lackluster.

A note about durability. As I was finishing up the testing of this camera I bobbled the camera due to nerve damage and it took a spill. The height was not great, less than three feet, and the initial impact was on soil and grass. The lens came apart into numerous pieces. I was able to put the lens back together but it appears to have suffered internal damage and will not focus either automatically or manually. I accept that I caused this damage but I am very unimpressed with the durability of such an expensive camera.

I really can't recommend this camera. Three stars but barely.

A side note about Samsung's technical support that isn't reflected in my rating of this camera. Calling Samsung's support line was a complete nightmare. Audio quality was atrocious. At the end I was practically screaming to be heard. I spent close to an hour and a half on the phone speaking with seven different people. Each person I spoke to had to be told all my information, the camera's information and the reason for my call. Four times I was transferred to 'the proper department.' In the end I had a supervisor tell me, first that the camera did not exist and then, that it must be a UK version and I'd have to start all over and call their UK support line. I then contacted Samsung through their Facebook support page. It's been almost a week and they still haven't decided what to do about the camera/lens.

{Edit}
It took nearly a month of back and forth and arguing to get Samsung to agree my camera was a US version, it was under warranty and they would issue a repair ticket for it. It was shipped off at their expense, repaired surprisingly quickly and shipped back. The camera's now in working order. Only one thing marred the process. When they returned the camera and lens the put a cap on the rear of the lens (I'd shipped it with the lens attached) but only put a piece of what looked like a Post-It across the body opening. I found it odd they wouldn't properly cap the body to protect the sensor though on the whole the packing job, bubble wrapped and foam peanuts was well done. Kudos to their repair facility but I'm still very put off by the whole experience with their support people.

title: Sophie and Sadie really liked this food; it is a supplement to their diet
text:
I got this for my friend's dogs to supplement with their other food.  Both Sofie and Sadie really liked this food. I personally like the large kibble size.

Note that unless a dog has a grain allergy, it is not a good idea to feed them grain-free foods exclusively. The reason is that vets are finding an association between heart disease (such as canine dilated cardiomyopathy) and grain-free dog foods. However, it is mostly associated with the foods that have peas, lentils, other legumes or potatoes as their main ingredients. Note that I did not see any of the "bad" ingredients in this food; however, I personally would only supplement a dog's diet with grain-free since the science is new even though I really like the ingredients in this food. I also believe variety is best for nutrition.

This food's first 15 ingredients are deboned chicken, egg, sweet potato, tapioca, chicken fat, natural chicken flavor, dicalcium phosphate, minerals, flaxseed, yeast hydrolysate, cranberries, blueberries, broccoli, dandelion greens, salt, etc.

title: The PERFECT computer stand!

I use a computer stand/table in the living room so I can watch television and just have a better outdoor view (the view from my office isn't great, and my living room window overlooks a park-like yard). I've been using a much fancier (and more expensive) "computer stand" for a couple of years, but it finally bit the dust (the weld that holds the desktop onto the central support column failed). So I started the search for a replacement, one that maybe wasn't so fancy but would last longer.

Of course I came to Amazon -- they have everything! -- and found a number of options. This looked like the best fit, so I ordered it.

I'm absolutely thrilled with it. Seriously, it's even better than I expected, even with my experience with Lifetime tables (which has been excellent). This little table is the PERFECT size for my laptop, a mug of coffee, and a couple of other items (reading glasses, etc.). It's lightweight enough that I can easily scoot it out of the way when I need to move around (get a coffee refill, etc.). My only quibble is that I wish it came in black, but that's absolutely NOT a deal breaker.

This feels far more stable than my old computer stand even when it was new, and it's not likely to have any similar problems. I love that I can adjust the height, too.

Overall, this is a solid 5-star item. Would happily purchase again if the need arises.

Context: I have have an '05 Subaru Outback Limited, which has a 6-CD changer but no cassette deck or AUX-in. I have a decent amount of experience in audio, low-voltage electric, and soldering.

ASIN of other parts I purchased:

RCA-3.5mm cable: B00LM2Y2U4
3.5mm panel-mount jack: B00OGLCR3W
Antenna adapters for Subaru: B000K53QBA
3.5mm braided, right-angle cable: B01K3WYKW8

I installed this in my Outback after thinking about doing so for years. I've never used the sound system in my car and it felt like a bit of a waste, and I would like to listen to audiobooks and music on my commute or long trips. Previously I considered tying the audio into the wiring harness for the CD player in order to attain maximum quality, but it was sufficiently unapproachable that I put it off for years. I ended up going with the iSimple instead of a generic FM transmitter because I wanted to get the maximum possible quality at the maximum power, hopefully improving the battery life of my MP3 player (a Sandisk Sansa Clip+).

As for installation: I watched a video on Youtube by a guy named Dirtcheapdaily (How to add an auxiliary port to any car | Ep.81) which made the process very simple. It took me about three hours total from start to finish, and required that I remove the center console from the car and make some modifications on the workbench. However, I wanted my car to look stock, with everything hidden away - if you don't care about any of that, you could literally do this in 20m.

However, the steps I took were: remove some panels from center console and radio - pull antenna wires out from behind head unit- connect iSimple model to antenna wires via adapters to check length of wires - remove center console and bring to workbench - add velcro and attach iSimple to space inside center console where it won't interfere with anything - drill holes in wall of center console storage compartment - cut switch wires, feed through holes, resolder w/ heatshrink - feed audio wire through hole, solder to 3.5mm jack, seat in hole - trim, then solder power wires to back of cigarette lighter (only has power when ACC is on) - tie all wires down so they don't wander - return center console to car and temporarily reconnect to adjust gain and switch to best radio station, and make sure parking brake doesn't interfere with modules or wires - reassemble car and test one last time.

Regarding quality: after adjustment, I'd say the audio quality is pretty good. When the switch is on, there is no interference whatsoever from other stations. It is not as good as a true line in, but I don't see that as being very important as I frequently have the windows down, hear road noise, or have the car vents running, so for me fairly good is good enough. It is better than many external FM transmitters I've heard, and much more consistent.

I do wish the gain on the unit was a bit stronger, I have it maxed out an still have to crank my volume up to 50% if I have my MP3 player on ~50% volume, which isn't an issue it itself but at 20 the other radio stations are truly deafening. It is possible that the gain is limited by FCC regs, though. For now, I just set all my presets to the radio station I have selected on the unit to avoid accidentally shifting to a different one. This way I can run the MP3 on 50% and the battery will hold out longer than otherwise.

So, as for recommendations - I would say that if you want the best quality in the most unobtrusive form factor, this is a good investment so long as installing it into your car isn't -too- much of a hassle. I found the process educational myself but for some it might just be frustrating. If you just want audio and you aren't too attached to how you get it, I would order an external plug-in FM transmitter first and only upgrade if you feel it would be necessary.

title: Great value for the price; works flawlessly on PCs, with only a couple of minor issues
text: This is a review for the TK-408 switch.  I noticed the reviews seem to show up on several different models.  This model has the round PS/2 type connections for mouse and keyboard, and female connections for VGA. It also has audio connections, so you can use one set of speakers for several different computers. There are no USB connections on it.  All the cables are included.  I use this to switch between PCs; some reviewers mentioned trouble with MACs.  The only real issue I have encountered is that if I power up a computer that is off and I am currently switched to another computer, when I go back to the one that was off (that is now on), the screen resolution has dropped.  If I switch to the turned off computer while it still off and power up and boot up before switching away, there is no issue and then I can switch back and forth all day with everything staying as it should be.  It's just a very minor annoyance.  If the computers you are switching between are always on, it would never be an issue.  The other thing that I found out is that for me the audio was not of much use.  The reason is that I am often listening to music on one computer; when I wanted to switch to another computer to do some work, the sound stopped, obviously because now I was on another computer that didn't have music playing.  I ended up just hooking up 3 sets of speakers for my 3 computers.  A lot of space used up, but a better solution for me.  The sound situation is not a problem with the switch, as it was doing exactly what it should by looking for output from the line out on the computer that you are switched to.  Some reviewers mentioned problems with delay in the hotkey switching.  I haven't noticed this and usually it takes no more than one second to switch.  My switch uses ScrLk twice followed by the port number the computer is on.  I have tried out two more expensive switches that don't have hotkey capability and you have to press a button on the switch.  With Trendnet switches, you can do either - use the keyboard sequence or press the physical key on the switch.  I have had this switch in service for a number of years and the only physical issue I have encountered is that once in a while the master keyboard and mouse connections loosen up and have to be re-seated.  The switch has given me many years of flawless operation and so far has proven to perform better than much more expensive switches.  Very good value for the price and I highly recommend it.  I like Trendnet equipment so far and have some other products of theirs that also work very well.

title: Creative potential is what sold me
text:
Truly what's not to love? This is the perfect desk top computer for your college student. It's also the perfect desktop for any business with a marketing department. I watched this video and was totally hooked. I have been doing PowerPoint presentations for 24 years and this blows it out of the water.

What finally hooked me to it's creative potential at the office was watching two 3 minute videos on YouTube:
"HP Sprout Review" and "Using the Capture Feature on Sprout by HP" - amazing

Hook up was easy as I expected about 20 minutes to unbox everything and less than an hour to get everything running

Now, right now I am not in a financial picture to buy the 3D printer or imaging stand (even tho the prices are not outrageous),but I can still get a designed printed by establishing a free account with HP's 3D printing partner. FYI the Dremel is the highest rated model by '3D Engineer' just go to their sight and search "dremel-idea-builder-review" it gave me a lot of easily understandable information if I decide to go that route. You can also go to the Dremel site '3dprinter dot dremel' the videos there helped me learn a lot about how this 3D printing works. Lastly, I read a informational article at 'makezine' that you can find on the internet "dremel-3d-printer-idea-builder".

Ok, so the next stop on my journey of discovery was HP where I searched 'Sprout'. So I watched the videos and skimmed the tech stuff. WELL worth your time - I truly think it saved me a TON of time. If object design is your thing or you are looking to get your high school or college kid into computer design this desk top will hook them. It's just so creative! One tip when getting started, on the HP site I put a query of "Sprout" in the search engine and got a nice small list of use links PLUS a dedicated SPROUT FORUM for users where HP folks jump in all the time with helpful information and trouble shooting help.

Ok, I really wanted to so how the 3D works so I created a free account with the HP 3D printer partner Sculpteo - it could not be easier. First stop for me was searching the Sculpteo site for '3D Printing Price and Payment Methods' and 'help/#price-calculation'. You can see it doesn't have to be ridiculously expensive - but it can be - the larger the object the bigger the cost. The site is very user friendly and immersive, even if you don't plan to print right off take a look, it is fascinating. A very good article "Sculpteo Opens its 3D Printing Cloud Engine to the Public, BY ANDREW WHEELER MAY 8, 2015" explained how this all works. Also "HP & Sculpteo Partner to 3D Print Directly from Sprout BY DAVIDE SHER AUGUST 3, 2015". Both are most helpful. If you care to read super there are 3 other articles about Sculpteo I read:

Sculpteo: French, Web-Based 3D Printing Service Sculpteo Puts Down Roots in Silicon Valley by Debra Thimmesch | Sep 30, 2015
Staples’ New Sculpteo-Powered Online 3D Printing Service Launches by Scott J Grunewald | Sep 17, 2015

Finally go to you tube and watch a demo "Baig: Here's what HP's new Sprout can do".

I did all this reading and watching while I was waiting for the 55 pound box to arrive and have been playing with it the last 30 days with no complaints at this time. I have only used the presentation creation piece so far but once my college kid gets his hands on it this summer I expect a lot of creativity that should be pretty cool.

title: Whoa- this is an upgraded mini PC! Twice the specs, and finally a USB type C!
text:
I love mini PCs. I use them for all kinds of projects, from digital signage to file servers and attached to TVs to make them media consumption units. Usually they are somewhat low powered, running a slightly older architecture chip like a Celeron J4125, and low ram/storage limits to the soldered on chips. For simple computing tasks, they do a good job as long as you don't expect too much of them.

But this one is SPECIAL! First of all, can I get an AMEN on finally recognizing the need to give us a USB type C port on one of these boxes? For specs, the N5095 is easily 30% faster in benchmarks to most of my other mini PCs, and has twice the ram and storage! At 16GB and a 512GB SSD, the specs are starting to look closer to my work laptop than a cheap media center box. This box also has the usual perks of a mini PC like a SATA port for an add-on drive, although with 512GB of storage you won't be needing it as often as those 128GB storage cheap boxes. I've used Beelink boxes before, and I've always found them to be decent quality, from their Android MXQ media boxes to these newer Mini PCs, I'm excited to see how far they've come in replacing the standard desktop for an ever expanding variety of users!

title: Works with Android Auto!

I have an Android Auto head unit in my car, but it requires a direct connection to my phone to work. When I'm in a hurry, I usually throw my phone in the holster of the car and start driving... I used this 100 foot cable to run between my router to a PoE switch that branches to several power and transmit data to and from one zone of my security cameras - a primary connection where speed and a reliable relay is critical - and I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

This has proven to be an outstanding, dependable Ethernet Cable - this is really a top of the line cable that you’ll love.

title: FANTASTIC SOUND BAR with a remote that is an absolute disaster.  Fix the remote and 5-STARS no question.
text:
The sound from this bar is clean, clear, crisp and LOUD! A very decent amount of BASS, with a sub woofer output should you want to connect one. I found out I ordered a longer bar than is recommended. How did I find out? The packaging for this bar states that it is for a 42" or larger TV. I purchased it for a 32" TV. The concern, I believe, is that if the speakers are too far from the TV's center it will not seem as though the audio is coming from the actors. My brain is making the leap and tricking me so all is well. I use my TV for music for the most part anyway (Comcast Music Choice and Fire TV Music).
It is disappointing that Fire TV Music has such poor audio quality since it is there that I can make personal music choices unlike Comcast. Fire TV just sounds plain bad. It did on the TV speakers and now on the bar; it is just un-listenable. Safe to call it "LOW FIDELITY"
As far as connecting an input to this bar from your TV you have many options and most all the cables you may need are included. I really liked that they included the cord to to connect the bar to a sub. This cord is over and above what is required to connect the bar to the TV...very nice touch VIZIO. Now I need to go to my storage and try to find my sub :-)
My TV only offers 2 audio outputs, head phone and optical. Included with the bar were a headphone-to-2 RCA connector cord, and a fiber optic patch cord, among others. That allowed me what would be considered the worst quality connection and the best quality connection possibilities. If you don't have OPTICAL OUT on your TV do not despair...the worst possible option (headphone-to-RCA patch cord) sounds FANTASTIC! I can detect no loss of fidelity between the two. You will not be missing out.
Now to the reason I gave it 3 stars rather than 5. The back of the remote just keeps sliding off. It is not broken in any way. Just poorly designed. I often use the sound bar in dark or nearly dark conditions. It is taking time to train myself to not go where I normally would to use the any of the buttons. So how about the POWER button? It is not the top left button on the remote as you will see and are used to on any other remote in your home. For some strange reason instead of the power button being in the far upper left of the remote they felt this was a good place to position the INPUT button. Power is upper right. Volume UP/DOWN is traditionally placed on the left side of the remote with a paddle switch or separate buttons. Located in the standard volume UP/DOWN positions are the TruVolume and the TruSurround HD. The volume UP/DOWN are located on a FLAT 1-3/8" (34.9mm) x 1-3/8" (34.9mm) multi-function EVER SO SLIGHTLY RAISED square. To be honest I can't even tell that it IS raised at all most of the time. If you go for the volume in low light you may operate any of 3 other function controls. Lastly, if you were hoping the VOLUME controls are the 2 well raised buttons on the right (traditional location) you would be wrong. Those are your BASS/TREBLE controls.
I am not sure I would buy this bar again knowing what I do now about the remote. As I said I often use the remote in low or no light. The problems I mention here may just be my own...but I doubt it. All of these tiny buttons and controls are all scrunched into a small 2-3/8" (60.3mm) x 1-3/8" (34.9mm) upper 40% of this little remote and they are not raised enough and not far apart enough to be used just by touch. I well believe that just 3 functions on the remote will account for 90% of it's use. POWER (that CAN be felt but it is in the wrong place...you'll get used to that) and the VOLUME UP/DOWN that exist on a square, fully smooth (NO tactile feedback...I'd hate to see a blind person trying to operate), 4-function piece of plastic that is raised about 1/32" (0.8mm). On the bright side for me, I found out fairly quickly that my cable box remote controls the basic functions of the sound bar. I hope you get so lucky.
Knowing what I know now I should have purchased a bar in the 28"-32" (71mm-81mm) class looking for features such as the control panel on the bar being mildly illuminated and a proper remote perhaps with illumination itself. My roommate may buy mine from me for a location that is always well lit and has a 42" TV. I'll lose $20 on the deal but I can get the absolute right bar for me.. I don't return items that are not what I would like due to my own failure in researching. So, for better or worse, the bar is mine. There is one thing you cannot fault; THIS THING SOUNDS AMAZING!
- Good Shopping!!!

title: A review from someone who is actually playing it....not just saying my kid likes it...and a bit of comparison to the 3ds version
text: Love it.  Great graphics, fun modes and lots to do. Terrific voice acting and characters.  I have the 3ds version and the portal works fine with the PS3.  The console version really is a whole lot better than the 3ds version but the 3ds version is more of a platformer, you can store two Skylanders and just swap them out by tapping their icon on the bottom screen and they can jump.  Other than that, the PS3 version is a much more immersive and richer game.  I think this is a game for the whole family to enjoy and I have played a heck of a lot of games since 1978.  Infact, it sort of reminds me of old fashioned Diablo type dungeon crawling (and some Skylanders have similar type abilities) but most of the adventuring takes place in well lit areas and even though the NPCs are cute they are not "sticky sweet" or too childish for adults who just want to experience a fun game. I love the bright colors and the little details like ice forming on the ship...or little puddles on the deck.  And it is FUN. I like buying the character updrades in this version as that is not an option but is automatic in the 3ds version.  Skylanders transferred from the 3ds retain their LEVELS but not their upgrades.  Hats in this version actually have a purpose and can effect stats in many different ways such as making a Skylander faster or better defensively.  In the 3ds version hats just sit on their heads and look cool...lol....no effects at all.  I waited for this version and the figures to become a little more affordable and honestly, it's one of those rare times I wish I had just bought it on release day because it's that good and would have been well worth the price. Finding new figures in the stores is almost impossible now. Good news-- It's ok to buy Skylanders used if you want to or don't have a bunch of cash....this version has an option to reset the Skylander so you can do all its stats, leveling up yourself.  Also...the best thing about BOTH games....you really only have to have 1 giant and a Skylander of each element to play the game effectively and enjoy all the parts.  So...I think that comes down to your giant and 7 of the other elements.  And since you can use Skylanders from the original game, there's lots to pick from and enjoy.  Of course, you'll want more than 8 but it's like eating an elephant---ONE bite at a time will get you there :)  At first I thought the figures were a horrible gimmick idea but now that more and more games on any system are requring you to pay for additional DLC...this is really cool since you have a figure and a game character to show for your money spent.  There's no online mode for the battle arenas....that's the only thing I don't like about this game. I've been fairly dependent on online for quick games with other people for several years so no online battle option feels like a step backwards in gaming.  Other than that, i think the concept is amazing, the game plays very well, the modes mix it up, replay value is strong for each level and for each figure you collect.  I think it's superb and would think anyone who likes games could enjoy this nearly perfect game.

I would not feed this to male cats as the dry nature can make them more prone to crystals in the urine. However, in tiny amounts as a treat only, it will work well with home made food.

DO THE CATS LIKE IT?
Both of our cats are used to home made food (we always add proper amounts of nutrients including taurine) so they don't tend to like a lot of processed foods for long periods of time. This time, however, I found that as a treat a few times a week, both cats love these.

THE BOTTOM LINE
As a food, I do not recommend this- it is WAY too expensive. As a treat to have on hand and give occasionally in smal amounts, yes. Our cats do like it.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS when used as a treat. As a regular food, it is just too expensive.

title: So far, so good!
text:
It's only been about a week, but I'm very happy with this keyboard so far. I'm a writer who spends roughly eight hours a day, sometimes seven days a week at the keyboard. This one is responsive and gives me that satisfying click-clack this typewriter-training typist loves - some might find it annoying, though, and the space bar is particularly loud. That did throw me a bit at first.

I tried four different ergonomic setups with this before I found one that didn't result in hand fatigue: keyboard alone, both with the legs up and down, and then keyboard with wrist rest, legs both up and down. What finally worked for me was legs up and a wrist rest. I don't see this working without a wrist rest for any programmer or writer.

I'm also impressed with the battery life. I haven't recharged since I had it, though, granted I don't use the lights. I honestly didn't mean to let it go this long but I keep forgetting to plug it in at night despite the sticky note on my desk.

As other reviewers have mentioned, it's heavy. For me, that's a good thing because it doesn't slide around. I can't see traveling with it, though.

I also like the build. Unlike the last mechanical keyboard I had, which lasted only a couple of years, these keys are less gappy. That's perfect for someone with the unfortunate habit of eating at the desk no matter how many times I tell the kids to not do that because it trashes your keyboard. ;)

What would it take to make it a five for me? Probably a built-in wrist rest though, at this price point, I'm not complaining. I'm very happy with it.

title: I'm really liking the Ulanzi brand
text:
When I purchased the [[ASIN:B08RRV6S6W Ulanzi battery handle]] to go with my DJI pocket, I was impressed with the quality of the product. When gathering together my camera gear for my vacation, I realized that I actually purchased a couple of other Ulanzi products previously. Since then, this brand has jumped out at me when looking for camera accessories.

This ULANZI MT-33 Camera Tripod had a convenience feature that I didn't realize it had when I ordered it. It is well thought out and has good build quality (with one minor caveat). It is a flexible tripod that is strong enough to hold my mirrorless Lumix camera and is equipped with a cold shoe socket as well as a 1/4" screw hole. The cold shoe can hold a microphone or small LED video light which the 1/4" screw hole can either mount another cold shoe or other camera accessories.

The convenience feature that I didn't know about is that the mounting head of this tripod can open up to become a phone holder. It's not a separate accessory that screws on to the quarter inch screw. The spring-loaded phone holder is actually part of the mounting head's design. What this means is that one can switch from taking pictures with a camera to filming with a cell phone without fumbling around with phone brackets.

In my pictures, you will see a screw with its tightening wheel. The screw is supposed to be securely seated in the wheel but it wasn't seated properly in the product I received and it came apart. It wasn't a big problem. Simply reassemble the screw and wheel back and then mount a camera to the tripod. By tightening the screw to the camera and keep turning. The tightening action will seat the screw back into the wheel and should not come out anymore.

I'm not a video blogger but it seems like I'm slowly collecting many accessories that make me think perhaps it's a shame for me not to be? I have the necessary tools for it... not everyone is made to be in front of the camera, I guess.

The folks at Roxant have thought of everything! I wanted a monocular because I only have sight in one eye. I wanted a lightweight scope I could hold and focus with the same hand. I love the focus wheel and the hand strap. When the strap is tight, I don’t even need to grip the scope, just lift it and hold it against my eye.

The tripod is a bit flimsy, but probably stable enough for light use. In any case, it doesn’t take any space in the case and doesn’t add any weight, so I pack it in with the scope. Sometimes I use it as a handle for the scope and it works well.

But here’s the best part: the optics are great! I have an Eagle Solo which just isn’t stable enough against my eye for me to enjoy, and is a pain to focus. The Roxant Falcon gives me just as good vision and magnification as the Eagle. At a fraction of the price, especially when considering the accessories!

I hesitated to order this, since I had a good quality monocular already, but it had so many features I wanted from a monocular (focus wheel, strap, accessories), for the price I figured I’d give it a try. It vastly exceeded my expectations. It will now be my go-to scope for everything.
